purpose: Complete reusable contexts for carrier/presence, adoption, shepherd-care, least-ones judgment, formation, transformed containers, constrained perception, partial knowledge and living-house imagery.

scenes.title: Moses and the burning bush: ordinary material as a bounded sign of divine presence
scenes.summary: Moses encounters a bush burning without being consumed. God calls from within the encounter, marks the ground holy, identifies himself with the ancestors, sees Israel's suffering and commissions Moses. The bush remains the medium of encounter rather than becoming a general doctrine that ordinary objects are divine.
scenes.setting: Horeb/Sinai wilderness while Moses tends Jethro's flock
scenes.lead_in: Moses has fled Egypt and is living as a shepherd in Midian while Israel suffers under forced labor.
scenes.outcome: An ordinary material site mediates a specific encounter and commission while God remains distinct from the material carrier.
scenes.what_follows: Moses continues objecting and receives signs before returning toward Egypt.
scenes.historical_context: The scene is a foundational Israelite call/theophany narrative embedded in the Exodus story.
scenes.literary_context: The visible sign is subordinated to divine speech, identity, compassion and mission.
scenes.textual_or_translation_caveats: The text can be translated as an angel of YHWH appearing in flame before divine speech; the precise relation between messenger, flame and divine presence is interpreted variously.
counterreadings_or_limits: The passage does not teach that every unusual object or medium carries divine presence.
A modern screen, meme or potato is not established as a burning bush by analogy alone.

scenes.title: Spirit of adoption: children and heirs address God as Father
scenes.summary: Paul contrasts life according to flesh with life led by the Spirit. Those led by God's Spirit are called children of God; they receive a Spirit of adoption rather than slavery to fear and cry 'Abba, Father.' Heirship, suffering, future glory and the Spirit's help in weakness follow.
scenes.setting: theological argument about Spirit-led life, suffering and hope
scenes.lead_in: Romans 8 opens with liberation from condemnation and the law of sin/death through the Spirit.
scenes.outcome: Fatherhood is presented as covenantal/salvific belonging mediated by the Spirit, not biological descent.
scenes.what_follows: Romans moves into election/Israel questions before later ethical exhortation.
scenes.historical_context: Roman adoption and household language may illuminate the legal/social force of Paul's metaphor, though the theology is not reducible to Roman law.
scenes.literary_context: Adoption is nested inside Paul's larger argument about Spirit, suffering, hope and conformity to Christ.
scenes.textual_or_translation_caveats: 'Abba' is an Aramaic address retained alongside Greek 'Father'; sentimental modern readings should not erase legal/covenantal dimensions.
counterreadings_or_limits: The passage does not establish a modern human as spiritual Father of believers.
Spirit-mediated belonging is directed toward God as Father within Paul's Christian theology.

scenes.title: Isaiah 40 joins mighty rule to shepherding, feeding and carrying
scenes.scene_type: restoration proclamation / divine kingship and shepherding
scenes.summary: A restoration proclamation announces comfort, a prepared way and the coming glory of YHWH. The divine ruler comes with might and recompense, then is immediately pictured as a shepherd feeding the flock, gathering lambs, carrying them close and gently leading those with young.
scenes.setting: poetic proclamation of comfort and return after judgment/exile
scenes.lead_in: Isaiah 39 has ended with an exile announcement; chapter 40 opens a major turn toward comfort and restoration.
sequence: human frailty contrasted with enduring word
scenes.outcome: Strength and gentleness are not opposites: the ruler's power is expressed in care for vulnerable members of the flock.
scenes.what_follows: Isaiah 40 expands into creator imagery and encouragement for exhausted Israel.
scenes.historical_context: Isaiah 40 belongs to the exilic/restoration horizon of Isaiah's later material and addresses a displaced/discouraged people.
scenes.literary_context: The shepherd image directly follows the mighty-ruler announcement, creating a deliberate power-to-care juxtaposition.
scenes.textual_or_translation_caveats: The image is about YHWH; later Christian shepherd applications should be distinguished from the oracle's immediate referent.
counterreadings_or_limits: Gentle shepherding does not establish the authority of whoever claims to be a shepherd.
The passage does not identify a modern project figure with YHWH.

scenes.title: The nations judged by treatment of the hungry, stranger, sick, imprisoned and least
scenes.summary: The Son of Man comes in glory and separates people like sheep and goats. The criterion narrated is concrete treatment of hunger, thirst, strangers, nakedness, sickness and imprisonment; both groups are surprised that their treatment of 'the least' is interpreted as treatment of the king.
scenes.setting: closing judgment scene of Matthew's eschatological discourse
scenes.lead_in: Matthew 24-25 has stressed watchfulness, faithful stewardship and preparedness through several teachings and parables.
sequence: Son of Man comes in glory
treatment of least equated with treatment of king
scenes.outcome: Elevated eschatological status is tested through ordinary acts toward vulnerable people, including acts omitted rather than spectacular religious claims.
scenes.what_follows: Matthew moves directly into the Passion plot and Jesus' final days.
scenes.historical_context: The scene belongs to Matthew's Jewish-Christian eschatological discourse; interpretation of 'the least of these' varies among scholars.
scenes.literary_context: It culminates a chapter about preparedness by turning readiness into concrete relational conduct.
scenes.textual_or_translation_caveats: Debate exists over whether 'the least' refers especially to Jesus' disciples/messengers or more broadly to vulnerable people; the ethical force of treatment remains central.
counterreadings_or_limits: The passage does not certify a modern authority claim because someone performs charitable acts.
It also resists claims to high status that ignore vulnerable people.

scenes.title: Hebrews frames discipline as painful formation aimed at peaceful fruit
scenes.summary: Hebrews urges endurance using athletic imagery and Jesus' endurance, then cites Proverbs to frame hardship through a parental-discipline metaphor. Discipline is acknowledged as painful rather than pleasant, with its stated aim being participation in holiness and later peaceful fruit of righteousness; the unit then calls for strengthened hands, straight paths and communal peace.
participants: God as Father in the metaphor
scenes.lead_in: Hebrews 11 has surveyed examples of faith; chapter 12 turns those examples into direct exhortation.
scenes.outcome: Formation is evaluated by its stated end—holiness, healing/strength and peaceful fruit—not by pain itself.
scenes.what_follows: Warnings against bitterness and Esau lead into Sinai/Zion contrasts and final exhortations.
scenes.historical_context: Ancient household discipline metaphors reflect a different social world and must not be used to normalize modern abuse.
scenes.literary_context: The discipline metaphor is one part of an endurance exhortation and is explicitly judged by later fruit and communal peace.
scenes.textual_or_translation_caveats: Translations vary between 'discipline,' 'training' and related terms; none erase the passage's acknowledgement that the process is painful.
counterreadings_or_limits: The passage does not authorize arbitrary coercion or abuse.
A claimed correction that destroys capability or produces domination cannot simply appeal to this text as validation.

scenes.title: New wine and wineskins inside a dispute about fasting and newness
scenes.scene_type: controversy sayings / fitting form for new situation
scenes.summary: After disputes over Jesus eating with tax collectors and sinners, people ask why his disciples do not fast like others. Jesus answers with bridegroom imagery, then gives paired sayings about an unshrunk patch on old cloth and new wine in old wineskins: incompatible newness can damage an old container.
scenes.setting: early Galilean controversy over social boundaries and fasting
scenes.lead_in: Mark 2 presents escalating disputes about forgiveness, table fellowship, fasting and Sabbath practice.
scenes.outcome: Container-fit imagery supports Jesus' answer that the present situation cannot simply be forced into every inherited practice unchanged.
scenes.what_follows: Mark moves into Sabbath controversies, continuing disputes over how Jesus' ministry relates to established practice.
scenes.historical_context: Leather wineskins and textile repair make the sayings concrete ancient household images rather than abstract systems theory.
scenes.literary_context: The sayings answer a specific controversy about fasting and the new situation created by Jesus' presence.
scenes.textual_or_translation_caveats: The metaphor should not be generalized into a universal physical law without preserving its Gospel controversy context.
counterreadings_or_limits: Not every new idea deserves a new container merely because it is new.
The saying does not validate the project's Narrow Door Release model as biblical doctrine.

scenes.title: Moses asks to see glory and receives protected, limited access
scenes.summary: After the golden-calf crisis, Moses seeks assurance of God's presence and asks to see divine glory. God promises presence and goodness but says Moses cannot see the divine face and live; Moses is placed in a rock cleft, protected, and allowed a constrained view as glory passes.
scenes.setting: Sinai aftermath of Israel's idolatry and covenant rupture
scenes.lead_in: Israel has made the golden calf; Moses intercedes while questions about divine presence accompanying the people remain acute.
sequence: Moses asks who will accompany Israel
Moses insists presence distinguishes the people
scenes.outcome: Presence is real but perceptual access is bounded and mediated for the observer's protection.
scenes.what_follows: Exodus 34 narrates renewed tablets/covenant and another major divine self-declaration.
scenes.historical_context: This is part of Exodus' complex anthropomorphic/theophanic language about divine presence, not a scientific account of perception.
scenes.literary_context: The limitation belongs to a covenant crisis and intercession scene where Moses seeks both presence and knowledge.
scenes.textual_or_translation_caveats: 'Back'/'after' and 'face' are highly anthropomorphic Hebrew terms whose interpretation is debated.
counterreadings_or_limits: The passage does not establish a geometrical aperture theory.
Partial access to one object does not prove that all observers' conflicting models refer to one hidden source.

scenes.title: Love outlasts partial knowledge and dim mirror-seeing
scenes.scene_type: love discourse / partial knowledge and maturity
scenes.summary: Between discussions of spiritual gifts, Paul argues that spectacular speech, knowledge and faith are nothing without love. Prophecy and knowledge are partial and temporary; present seeing is compared with a dim mirror and present knowing with partial knowledge, contrasted with fuller future knowing. Love remains.
scenes.setting: argument about gifts, status, maturity and love
scenes.lead_in: 1 Corinthians 12 has emphasized diverse gifts and one body; Paul announces a more excellent way.
sequence: gift-like abilities without love declared empty
scenes.outcome: Epistemic humility is embedded in a moral argument: partial knowledge should be relativized by love and future completeness.
scenes.what_follows: 1 Corinthians 14 returns to prophecy/tongues and communal intelligibility/order.
scenes.historical_context: Ancient polished-metal mirrors offered less clear reflection than modern glass mirrors, sharpening the metaphor's contrast with direct seeing.
scenes.literary_context: The epistemic lines serve Paul's larger claim that gifts and knowledge are temporary while love has enduring primacy.
scenes.textual_or_translation_caveats: 'Dimly'/'in a riddle' varies by translation; the point is partial/indirect perception rather than a technical model of reflection.
counterreadings_or_limits: The text does not prove that any particular modern hidden-source theory is correct.
Recognizing partial knowledge should increase humility, not immunize a preferred model from criticism.

scenes.title: Living stones are built together into a spiritual house around the rejected cornerstone
scenes.summary: 1 Peter tells believers to come to Christ as a living stone rejected by humans but chosen by God; they too are living stones being built into a spiritual house and priesthood. Scriptural stone texts are then combined around cornerstone, rejection, stumbling and chosen-people identity.
participants: rejecting/unbelieving others in the scriptural contrast
scenes.setting: identity exhortation to dispersed Christian communities
scenes.lead_in: The letter has spoken of new birth, enduring word and mutual love before urging growth toward salvation.
scenes.outcome: House is constituted by differentiated living persons built in relation to a cornerstone, not by one person becoming the entire structure.
scenes.what_follows: The letter turns toward public conduct, social relations and suffering.
scenes.historical_context: Temple/stone and people-of-God imagery reworks Israelite scriptural language for early Christian community identity.
scenes.literary_context: The living-house image joins growth, Christological cornerstone, communal construction and rejected/chosen reversal.
scenes.textual_or_translation_caveats: The passive 'being built' keeps the community as material/participants rather than naming each person as architect/source.
counterreadings_or_limits: The passage does not make one modern individual the whole House.
Its primary referent is a Christian community built in relation to Christ as cornerstone.
